note: Jowett's translation prints no Stephanus numbers. Each number was matched by content to Burnet's Greek, whose sections Perseus marks: the Greek that the quoted Jowett sentence translates was found in that section by script (st, below), and the number is never estimated. A section of short exchanges can run over several Jowett blocks, so a reference lists every block it needs (PLATO_ST) and opens the first. Plato is public domain, so he is quoted exactly from the bundled Jowett, each quotation under 15 words. Jowett's “absolute justice” renders dikaion auto, which the forms entry says. Interpretation is credited to named scholarship only. Three disputes are recorded open, one per entry. Links: forms ↔ universals (the universals entry already calls Plato's forms the paradigm of transcendent realism, glossary-route3.json); elenchus → forms (Woodruff §5: Allen 1970 reads the What-is-X assumption as an early theory of forms); elenchus ↔ tripartite-soul (Woodruff's introduction contrasts the unified soul of the shorter dialogues with the divided soul of the middle ones); forms ↔ tripartite-soul (both from the Republic; the soul's turn to the good, Rep. 518c, and the ruling part's knowledge, Rep. 442c).
disputes: forms: What do knowledge and opinion range over in Republic V? Allan Silverman (Stanford Encyclopedia, §12) sets out three readings of “is” in the argument of 476–480: existential, veridical and predicative. On the existential and predicative readings knowledge and belief are set over objects, and on the predicative reading those objects are distinct; that reading, in Silverman's words, “lends itself to a defense of the Two Worlds account”, which keeps Forms and sensible things strictly apart. Gail Fine (1978, 1990) reads the “is” as veridical: knowledge is set over “what is true”, its objects are propositions, the overlap of the two faculties counts in the reading's favour, and both Forms and sensible things can be known. Not settled.

elenchus: Does the elenchus prove anything? Paul Woodruff (Stanford Encyclopedia, §2) holds that Gregory Vlastos “has argued persuasively” that the elenchus supports Socrates' ethical doctrine; on Hugh Benson's reading “the method can do no more than convict a partner of confusion”. The Internet Encyclopedia's article finds Vlastos's constructive account “not widely accepted by scholars for several reasons”. A related dispute concerns the priority of definition, the principle that one must be able to define a virtue to know anything about it: Peter Geach attacked it as the Socratic fallacy (Woodruff, §4), and the Internet Encyclopedia reports that “Many scholars judge PD to be implausible or false”. Not settled.

tripartite-soul: How agent-like are the three parts? Eric Brown (Stanford Encyclopedia, §2.1) takes Socrates' descriptions at face value, so that each part “is like an independent agent” (citing Kamtekar, 2006), a strategy of explaining action by “subpersonal homunculi” which Brown, citing Burnyeat (2006), calls both appealing and problematic. Shields (2001) and Price (2009) read them as “merely conceptual parts, akin to subsets of a set”. Not settled.

new_d.text: Plato's name for what each thing is in itself, such as justice itself, beauty itself and equality itself: unchanging, grasped by thought, and shared in by the many things we perceive.

new_text.text: In the Phaedo Socrates asks Simmias, “Is there or is there not an absolute justice?” (Phaedo 65d), and Simmias agrees that there is, and an absolute beauty and good, none of which he has ever seen with his eyes.
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Jowett's “absolute” renders the Greek for “itself”: at 65d Burnet's text reads dikaion auto, “the just itself”.
new_text.quotes: words quoted from the source named

new_text.text: Equal sticks and stones “appear at one time equal, and at another time unequal” (Phaedo 74b), while the equal itself never appears unequal, so the sticks are “not the same with the idea of equality” (Phaedo 74c).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: All such equals “strive to attain absolute equality, but fall short of it” (Phaedo 75a).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Socrates argues that we must have known the equal itself before we first perceived equal things, since we refer them to it, and that what we call learning is the recovery of that earlier knowledge through the senses: “may not this be rightly termed recollection?” (Phaedo 75e).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: The argument begins from Cebes' reminder of Socrates' “favorite doctrine” that knowledge is recollection (Phaedo 72e); the Meno, where the doctrine is set out at length, is not in the library.
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Asked whether the essences are ever changed, Cebes answers, “They must be always the same” (Phaedo 78d), while the many beautiful men, horses and garments are “always in a state of change” (Phaedo 78e).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: These can be seen and touched, but “the unchanging things you can only perceive with the mind” (Phaedo 79a).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Later, giving his own account of causes, Socrates holds that a beautiful thing is beautiful “only in as far as it partakes of absolute beauty” (Phaedo 100c), and that “by beauty all beautiful things become beautiful” (Phaedo 100d).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Allan Silverman (Stanford Encyclopedia) reads the Phaedo's Forms as “beings that are what they are in virtue of themselves”, “immaterial, non-spatial and atemporal”, and offers “a relation between material particulars and Forms” as a first approximation of partaking.
new_text.quotes: scholarship quotations checked in the source named

new_text.text: In Republic V the lovers of sights and sounds delight in fine colours and forms, but “their mind is incapable of seeing or loving absolute beauty” (Rep. 476b).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Whoever takes beautiful things for beauty itself is dreaming: he is one “who puts the copy in the place of the real object” (Rep. 476c).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: The philosopher is awake, able “to distinguish the idea from the objects which participate in the idea” (Rep. 476c–d).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Knowledge “is relative to being” (Rep. 477b), and opinion turns out to lie between knowledge and ignorance (Rep. 478d).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Those who see many beautiful things but not beauty itself “may be said to have opinion but not knowledge” (Rep. 479e); those who see “the absolute and eternal and immutable” may be said to know (Rep. 479e).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: What this argument sets knowledge and opinion over is disputed: see the dispute below.
In Book VI Socrates says that Adeimantus has often been told “that the idea of good is the highest knowledge” (Rep. 505a).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: The many beautiful and good things, he says, “are seen but not known”, and their ideas “are known but not seen” (Rep. 507b).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: The sun gives visible things their visibility and their growth, and the good, in the same way, imparts truth to the known and the power of knowing to the knower (Rep. 508e), and gives the objects of knowledge their being; yet “the good is not essence, but far exceeds essence in dignity and power” (Rep. 509b).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Silverman observes, citing Gerasimos Santas (1980), that Plato “never says in what sense the Good is responsible” for “the knowability and being of the objects of knowledge”.
new_text.quotes: scholarship quotations checked in the source named

new_text.text: Next comes “a line which has been cut into two unequal” parts, the visible below and the intelligible above, each cut again in the same proportion (Rep. 509d).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: In the lower intelligible part the soul uses visible things as images and reasons from hypotheses down to conclusions (Rep. 510b), as geometers do; in the higher, dialectic uses hypotheses “as steps and points of departure” toward “the first principle of the whole” and ends in ideas (Rep. 511b–c).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: To the four parts answer four states of the soul, noēsis, dianoia, pistis and eikasia in Burnet's Greek, which Jowett gives as reason, understanding, faith and “perception of shadows” (Rep. 511d–e).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Silverman reports that what the objects of dianoia are is a matter of great controversy, and cites Myles Burnyeat (1987) for the leading approaches.
Book VII pictures human beings who have lived from childhood in an underground den (Rep. 514a), chained so that “they see only their own shadows, or the shadows of one another” (Rep. 515a).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: A prisoner freed and dragged up into the light sees first shadows, then reflections, then the things themselves, the heavens by night, and last the sun itself (Rep. 516a–b).

Socrates applies the image: the prison is the world of sight, and the journey upward is “the ascent of the soul into the intellectual world” (Rep. 517b), where “the idea of good appears last of all” (Rep. 517b–c).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Education on this account turns the whole soul around, since “the power and capacity of learning exists in the soul already” (Rep. 518c), and needs an art of “conversion” (Rep. 518d).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Those who have seen the good must take their turn and “go down to the general underground abode” to rule (Rep. 520c).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_d.text: Socrates' way of examining a claim to know, as Plato portrays it: the speaker's answer to a question such as “What is piety?” is tested against other things the speaker agrees to until the two are shown to conflict.

new_text.text: In the Apology Socrates traces his questioning to Delphi, where Chaerephon asked the oracle whether anyone was wiser than Socrates, and “the Pythian prophetess answered, that there was no man wiser” (Apology 21a).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Puzzled, since he knew “that I have no wisdom, small or great” (Apology 21b), he went to a politician with a reputation for wisdom, hoping to refute the oracle.
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: The man thought himself wise and was not, and Socrates concluded that he had the advantage over him: “I neither know nor think that I know” (Apology 21d).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Poets and craftsmen fared no better, and he took the oracle to mean “that God only is wise” (Apology 23a), and that the wisest man is the one who, like Socrates, knows that his wisdom “is in truth worth nothing” (Apology 23b).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: He calls himself “a sort of gadfly, given to the state by God” (Apology 30e), and tells the jury that “the unexamined life is not worth living” (Apology 38a).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Paul Woodruff (Stanford Encyclopedia) thinks some form of elenchus probably lies behind Socrates' report that everyone he examined who claimed wisdom was found wanting.
The Euthyphro shows the method at work on one question.
Socrates asks, “And what is piety, and what is impiety?”, assuming that piety is “in every action always the same” (Euthyphro 5d).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Euthyphro answers from his own case, prosecuting his father for the death of a serf: “Piety is doing as I am doing” (Euthyphro 5d).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Socrates reminds him that he had asked him to “explain the general idea which makes all pious things to be pious” (Euthyphro 6d), something to serve as “a standard to which I may look” (Euthyphro 6e).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: The second answer, “Piety, then, is that which is dear to the gods” (Euthyphro 6e), fails because the gods quarrel, so that the same things are “both hateful and dear to them” (Euthyphro 8a).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Euthyphro amends it: “what all the gods love is pious and holy” (Euthyphro 9e).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Socrates then asks whether the holy is “beloved by the gods because it is holy”, or holy because it is beloved (Euthyphro 10a).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Euthyphro grants the first, “It is loved because it is holy, not holy because it is loved” (Euthyphro 10d), and so his definition, asked for the essence, gives “an attribute only” (Euthyphro 11a); in Burnet's Greek, ousia and pathos.
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: A third attempt makes piety “that part of justice which attends to the gods” (Euthyphro 12e), and ends as “learning how to please the gods in word and deed” (Euthyphro 14b), which brings the argument back to what is dear to the gods.
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: “Then we must begin again and ask, What is piety?” (Euthyphro 15c), Socrates says, and Euthyphro leaves.
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Woodruff calls the conclusion aporia, an impasse.
Woodruff sets out the requirements Socrates' question imposes: an answer must belong to every case of the virtue, to nothing that is not a case, and must explain why the cases are what they are.

The rules of the exchange are that the respondent “must answer every question according to his own beliefs”, and the questioner secures agreement to premises that turn out inconsistent with the first answer.
new_text.quotes: scholarship quotations checked in the source named

new_text.text: The Internet Encyclopedia's article gives Gregory Vlastos's statement of the pattern: the interlocutor “asserts a thesis, p”; “Socrates secures agreement to further premises, say q and r”; and the interlocutor agrees that q and r entail not-p.
new_text.quotes: scholarship quotations checked in the source named

new_text.text: It notes that “the Socratic method is sometimes dubbed the elenchus”, and that Socrates himself never gives his method that name.
new_text.quotes: scholarship quotations checked in the source named

new_text.text: Woodruff's puzzle is how the method could lead to “any firm result” when its premises “have no authority beyond the partner's agreement”.
new_text.quotes: scholarship quotations checked in the source named

new_d.text: Plato's account in Republic IV: the soul has three parts, reason, spirit and appetite, and a person is just when each part does its own work, with reason ruling.

new_text.text: In Book II Glaucon and Adeimantus press Socrates to show that justice is to be chosen for itself (Rep. II); Eric Brown (Stanford Encyclopedia) notes that “Socrates' strategy depends on an analogy between a city and a person.”
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script; scholarship quotations checked in the source named

new_text.text: In the city built in Books II–IV, justice turns out to be the principle laid down at its founding, that each should do the one thing his nature suits: “justice was doing one’s own business, and not being a busybody” (Rep. 433a).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Meddling among the three classes is the greatest harm to the city, and when traders, auxiliaries and guardians “each do their own business, that is justice” (Rep. 434c).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Socrates then asks whether the soul has the same three principles, warning that the present method is inadequate and “the true method is another and a longer one” (Rep. 435d).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: His test is a principle: “The same thing clearly cannot act or be acted upon in the same part” in contrary ways at the same time (Rep. 436b); Brown calls it the principle of non-opposition.
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script; scholarship quotations checked in the source named

new_text.text: A man may be thirsty and yet unwilling to drink (Rep. 439c), so the part that reasons and forbids differs from the part that thirsts, which Jowett calls “the irrational or appetitive” (Rep. 439d).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Leontius, passing the bodies of executed men, felt both a desire to see them and abhorrence; at last he ran to them crying, “Look, ye wretches, take your fill of the fair sight” (Rep. 440a).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: The moral is that “anger at times goes to war with desire” (Rep. 440a), and in such struggles “his spirit is on the side of his reason” (Rep. 440b).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Spirit is a third part, unless corrupted by bad education “the natural auxiliary of reason” (Rep. 441a), and so the principles in city and soul are agreed to be “three in number” (Rep. 441c).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: The individual is just in the same way as the city: one in whom “the several qualities of his nature do their own work will be just” (Rep. 441d–e).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Reason, wise and caring for the whole soul, should rule, with spirit as “the subject and ally” (Rep. 441e), and the two together govern appetite, “the largest part of the soul and by nature most insatiable of gain” (Rep. 442a).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: A person is courageous when spirit “retains in pleasure and in pain the commands of reason” about what to fear (Rep. 442b–c), wise by the ruling part's knowledge of what is “for the interest of each of the three parts” and of the whole (Rep. 442c), and temperate when all three “are equally agreed that reason ought to rule” (Rep. 442c–d).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: The city's division of labour “was a shadow of justice” (Rep. 443c); justice itself concerns the inner life, and the just man “is his own master and his own law, and at peace with himself” (Rep. 443d).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Injustice is “a strife which arises among the three principles” (Rep. 444b), and virtue is “the health and beauty and well-being of the soul” (Rep. 444d–e).
new_text.quotes: Plato's (Jowett) verbatim in the bundled book, inside the blocks their Stephanus reference opens; checked by script

new_text.text: Socrates checks the account against common cases: such a man is the least likely to make away with a deposit of gold or silver, or to commit theft, sacrilege or treachery (Rep. 442e–443a).

Brown credits David Sachs (1963) with the objection that this leaves unshown why a soul in such order will act justly in the ordinary sense, and judges that Socrates leaves the worry unaddressed at the end of Book IV, and Brown looks for answers in Books II–III and V–VII.
How agent-like the three parts are is disputed: see below.

summary: Three new entries read in Plato's own dialogues in the bundled Jowett: Forms (Phaedo and Republic V–VII, with the sun, line and cave), the elenchus (Apology and Euthyphro) and justice and the tripartite soul (Republic IV). 76 Stephanus numbers, each matched to Burnet's Greek and opening its passage in Jowett. Scholarship from Silverman (2014), Brown (2017), Woodruff (2022), Kraut (2026) and the Internet Encyclopedia. Three disputes recorded open: what Republic V's knowledge and opinion range over, whether the elenchus proves anything, and how agent-like the soul's parts are. The Socrates and Plato cards audited in thinkers-route.json.
